Agent Stack for ML Training Lifecycle:  
Generation, Validation, and Optimization

Jaideep Ray^(∗), Daniel Tang^(∗), Zejun Lin^(∗), Haoyue Tang^(∗), Lijuan
Zhang^(∗), Tao Huang^(∗), Tommy Li^(∗),  
Aditya Jain^(∗), Ankit Goyal^(∗), Harsh Jain^(∗), Zhuo Zhi^(∗), Youmin
Han^(∗), Santosh Jha^(∗), Shuying Liang^(∗),  
Yujie Ai^(∗), Jonathan Hung^(∗), Ethan Lyu^(∗), Abi Liu^(∗), Siddharth
Singh^(∗), Feng Wen^(∗), Mahesh Ravindran^(∗),  
Souvik Ray^(∗), Yitong Zhou^(∗), Animesh Singh^(∗)

LinkedIn • ^(∗)Equal contribution • Correspondence:
[jaray@linkedin.com](mailto:jaray@linkedin.com)

Abstract

Production model development requires repeated architecture design,
platform integration, debugging, training, and evaluation. We present an
agent stack deployed at LinkedIn with two independently usable agent
loops: AutoTorch for model generation and migration, and AutoResearch
for model optimization. AutoTorch generates PyTorch models and training
pipelines for TensorFlow migration, XGBoost replacement, and new-model
development. Executable validation hooks check platform API compliance,
trainability, and conversion fidelity on sampled data, guiding iterative
repair before engineer review and full-scale distributed training.
AutoResearch explores architecture and training-configuration changes
through expert-steered or autonomous experimentation. An external
orchestrator manages parallel trials, experiment history, candidate
selection, and wall-clock budgets across agent sessions. A shared
runtime preserves execution state independently of agent reasoning and
allocates GPUs separately from agent execution. Across ranking, content
understanding, and recommendation workloads, AutoTorch completed
generation and full-scale training in 92 of 115 workflow runs (80%). Of
these, 77 (83.7%) produced models meeting post-training quality
requirements. In a separate cohort, AutoResearch improved the primary
task metric on held-out data for 28 of 100 production pipelines.
Engineering teams estimate that the stack reduced elapsed end-to-end
migration time from approximately eight weeks to two weeks, a
$`4\times`$ speedup.

## 1 Introduction

Developing production machine learning models remains a labor-intensive
process. Engineers must design model architectures, integrate them with
platform-specific training APIs, debug runtime failures, and repeatedly
train and evaluate models to achieve target quality. Framework
migrations add further complexity, requiring engineers to reproduce
existing model behavior while adapting to a new training stack.

We introduce agent loops to automate this iterative process. Rather than
generating model code in a single step, agents continuously generate,
validate, repair, and optimize models using execution feedback. These
loops operate across multiple agent sessions and GPU training jobs, with
persistent state and validation mechanisms supporting long-running
execution (Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction")). We evaluate
this approach at LinkedIn across model generation, distributed training,
and offline evaluation.

We implement two independently usable agent loops. AutoTorch generates
PyTorch models and training pipelines, including framework migration,
and uses executable checks to guide repair before engineer review and
full-scale training. AutoResearch starts from a validated pipeline and
searches for improvements through budgeted experiments. Both can run
independently or be composed for migration followed by optimization.

A shared runtime supports these loops with durable execution sandboxes,
persistent task state, and brokered GPU and data access.
Architecture-specific skills guide candidate generation, while
executable validation and experiment records provide feedback to agents.
Completion remains governed by explicit checks and engineer review, not
by the LLM’s own assessment.

This paper describes three contributions: (1) model-generation and
optimization loops with task-specific validation and search policies;
(2) the shared runtime and execution controls supporting long-running
tasks on production training infrastructure; and (3) deployment
experience across model migration and optimization workloads at
LinkedIn.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 1: Model migration as a composition of independently usable agent
loops. AutoTorch generates a training model bundle; AutoResearch can
subsequently optimize the accepted model. Each loop also supports

## 2 Background and Problem

### 2.1 Production ML Pipelines

Production ML pipelines combine model architectures with preprocessing,
model-forward interfaces, data ingestion, distributed training
configurations, and offline evaluation APIs. At LinkedIn, agents must
follow these contracts to generate runnable training pipelines.

### 2.2 Migration as a Use Case

LinkedIn is migrating models from TensorFlow and XGBoost frameworks to a
PyTorch-based training stack. The migration also involves
framework-specific dependencies, including libraries such as TensorFlow
Ranking. We use this migration to exercise the agent loops across model
generation, validation, distributed training, and optimization.
AutoTorch generates and validates PyTorch models and training pipelines,
while AutoResearch searches for subsequent improvements. The loops can
also run independently.

### 2.3 Problem Formulation

We designed the system around two common ML engineering tasks. The first
is to generate a PyTorch model that works within the production training
platform and reaches the required task quality. The second is to improve
an existing model without disrupting its training and evaluation
pipeline.

Both workflows operate within the training and offline evaluation
lifecycle. API compliance includes the required preprocessing and
model-forward interfaces, but does not cover online serving integration,
latency or throughput SLAs, or A/B testing.

## 3 System Architecture

Each of the two agent loops consists of a set of task-specific skills
and an agent harness, and can run on general-purpose coding agents such
as GitHub Copilot and Claude Code. All agents run under LinkedIn
enterprise agreements. Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction")
shows the two loops composed for migration. The loops can also start
independently from a task specification, an experimental training
pipeline, or an accepted production model. Both run on a shared runtime
(Section [4](#S4 "4 Agent Control Plane")) and invoke the existing
production ML platform rather than a separate agent-specific training
stack.

### 3.1 AutoTorch Model Generation

AutoTorch generates trainable PyTorch models and their training
pipelines in two stages separated by engineer review
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Stage 2: full-scale training. ‣ 3.1 AutoTorch Model Generation ‣ 3 System Architecture")).
Stage 1 generates the model architecture and iteratively validates and
repairs it on a single GPU using sampled data. Once an engineer approves
the architecture, Stage 2 builds a Flyte training pipeline and runs
distributed training on multiple GPUs using production configurations
and the full-scale dataset. This separation allows agents to resolve
generation and validation failures before committing to full-scale
training.

For migration tasks, AutoTorch takes a source model and featurized data.
TensorFlow (TF) sources support weight transfer and parity checks, while
XGBoost sources provide task-quality targets. For new models, AutoTorch
uses a task specification and architecture-specific skills, including
wide and deep models, generative recommenders, graph neural networks,
TabM \[[7](#bib.bib7)\], and multi-task learning. The Stage 1 output is
a pull request containing generated code (model.py, train.py, data.py,
transforms.py, eval.py) and sampled validation results. The trained
checkpoint is produced in Stage 2.

#### Stage 1: sampled generation and repair.

For TensorFlow migration, the agent reconstructs the model in PyTorch,
transfers compatible parameters using deterministic analyzers or
agent-generated scripts, and applies lightweight output distillation
when some parameters cannot be mapped. Each iteration evaluates the
candidate on a sample of the featurized dataset. TensorFlow conversions
are scored on five dimensions: output parity (35%), task-metric parity
(20%), trainability (15%), code style (15%), and structural similarity
(15%). API compliance and trainability are also mandatory checks. A high
cloning match requires both checks and a composite score of at least 90:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
S_{\rm TF}=0.35P_{\rm io}+0.20P_{\rm task}+0.15T+0.15C+0.15H\geq 90.
``` |  | (1) |

Here, $`P_{\rm io}`$ and $`P_{\rm task}`$ denote output and task-metric
parity, while $`T`$, $`C`$, and $`H`$ denote trainability, code style,
and structural similarity, respectively. Each component is scored from 0
to 100.

Failed checks return scores and diagnostic evidence to the agent for
repair. For new models and XGBoost replacements, Stage 1 checks
generated-code validity, API compliance, trainability on sampled data,
and package/exportability before engineer review. Source-output parity
and the TensorFlow conversion score do not apply to these models.
Task-metric qualification follows full training, as described in
Section [5.7](#S5.SS7 "5.7 Multi-Dimensional Scoring ‣ 5 Model Generation and Validation").

Once the generated architecture passes its initial checks, AutoTorch
opens a pull request for engineer review. Stage 2 begins after approval.
Conversions scoring below 90 require explicit engineer approval and are
not counted as high cloning matches.

#### Stage 2: full-scale training.

The agent builds a Flyte-based trainer pipeline for the approved model
architecture and iterates until the component runs. The pipeline is
configured with the GPU count (n_gpus) and the full-scale dataset, and
packages the result as a torch package. Warm-start training from
transferred or distilled parameters can provide a fast check of
task-metric parity. Before downstream deployment, the model is trained
from a cold start using production configurations. The resulting
checkpoint is evaluated through the standard offline Evals API.

These stages measure different properties. Stage 1 evaluates conversion
fidelity by comparing the clone with the TF model on identical inputs.
Stage 2 verifies task quality after full-scale training, with cold-start
training establishing the final PyTorch model lineage.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 2: AutoTorch’s two stages. Stage 1 clones a TF model or builds a
new architecture, with sampled checks guiding repair. After engineer
review, Stage 2 can use a warm start for a fast task-metric check before

### 3.2 AutoResearch: Hill Climb on Validated Model

AutoResearch starts with a model that already has a working training and
evaluation pipeline. The agent proposes changes to the architecture or
training configuration, runs experiments, and compares the results
against the current best model.

Each candidate runs in a separate Git worktree branched from the same
incumbent, which remains fixed throughout the round. Experiments run in
parallel, but incumbent updates and the next round wait until all trials
in the current round have finished.
Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Experiment Orchestration ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research")
describes the selection policy.

#### Task.

The input is a validated model plus a research plan. The model is
supplied either as an existing Flyte training pipeline or as a GitHub
repository with the model code. The output has three parts: a
leaderboard of evaluated variants; a variant library of configurations,
architectures, and code branches; and a final report of findings, dead
ends, and a recommendation.

#### Research plan.

The research_plan.md specifies the training entry point, data, primary
metric, concurrency cap, and clock-hour budget. Engineers can provide
free-form research directions, such as which architectures to explore,
alternative losses or task-specific heads for multi-task learning, and
optimizer or training configurations. They can also specify changes to
avoid, such as feature crosses restricted by downstream serving
requirements. When no engineer-provided research focus is available, the
agent examines the model repository, training configuration, and prior
experiments to develop its own research directions.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 3: AutoResearch’s synchronous hill climb. A round begins from a
fixed incumbent, parallel trials run in separate worktrees, and
selection occurs after all results return.

## 4 Agent Control Plane

Coordinating agents is not the same as managing ML experiments.
Delegation alone does not track which model revision produced a metric,
enforce validation criteria, or preserve state across long-running GPU
jobs. Our loops keep validation results, experiment history, and
artifacts outside agent context, while a shared Kubernetes runtime
brokers GPU resources separately
(Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ LLM and agent configuration. ‣ 4 Agent Control Plane")).

#### Durable sandbox.

Agents execute in isolated Kubernetes pods backed by CPU or GPU
resources. Sandboxes provide network storage for plans, repositories,
and artifacts, with terminal session persistence and a seven-day
time-to-live (TTL). GPU jobs can be preempted when production workloads
need capacity. The agent client is not preempted, and its files and
experiment history remain available when GPU resources return.

#### Elastic warm GPU pool.

Agents release accelerators when idle, requesting experiment pods
dynamically via a broker backed by a warm H100/H200 pool. The control
plane borrows idle GPU capacity from production clusters under elastic
quotas, yielding capacity when production demand increases. This
decouples long-running agent lifecycles from accelerator allocation.

#### Controlled data and network access.

Training jobs launched by agents read production training data through
read-only, access-controlled paths; Member Data is not provided to the
LLM agents’ context. Operations such as trial submission and model
export use brokered services; deploying a model requires engineer
approval.

#### Memory.

The agentic job control plane logs all execution events and exposes a
unified memory interface. A shared console tracks runs, training jobs,
and metrics, maintaining artifact lineage back to originating
experiments. When human intervention is required, the runtime alerts the
owning team via chat while pausing the task without holding GPU
resources.

#### LLM and agent configuration.

We run AutoTorch with coding and reasoning agents through Copilot.
AutoTorch tasks must satisfy architecture, platform, and workflow
constraints using task-specific skills, tools, and validation hooks. In
AutoResearch, researcher, implementation, and evaluation roles can use
different agent configurations. Experiment state, time-budget
accounting, and candidate bookkeeping reside in the external
orchestrator.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 4: Durable agent sandboxes and independently allocated
accelerators. Training data is available only through controlled paths
and is not placed in LLM context.

## 5 Model Generation and Validation

### 5.1 Model Initialization

#### TensorFlow models.

For TensorFlow migrations, AutoTorch reconstructs preprocessing, feature
ordering, embeddings, network blocks, and output heads in PyTorch.
Parameter transfer uses deterministic analyzers and agent-generated
scripts. The analyzers match parameters using variable names, layer
types, indices, parameter roles, and tensor shapes, including layout
transposition when needed. When deterministic matching fails, the agent
generates custom transfer scripts to handle model-specific mappings.

When parameters cannot be mapped, AutoTorch falls back to lightweight
output distillation. A structural similarity score at or below 90%
indicates a low structural match. Distillation minimizes
variance-normalized mean squared error between the TensorFlow teacher
and PyTorch student predictions. The teacher is evaluated without
gradients, while the student’s BatchNorm layers are frozen and other
parameters remain trainable. By default, distillation runs for up to 500
steps with batch size 32, stopping early when the loss falls below
0.001. The default conversion path uses synthetic inputs.

#### No transferable state.

For non-cloneable models (e.g., XGBoost or custom frameworks), AutoTorch
constructs a PyTorch replacement and trains it directly on labeled data
using the source model solely as a quality benchmark.

#### New models.

For new model generation, AutoTorch uses task specifications, feature
schemas, target metrics, and permitted architecture families to build
and train candidate models using standard validation checks.

### 5.2 Platform API Compliance

Candidates must utilize supported platform APIs for data loading,
training, and evaluation. We verify compliance by executing generated
code against these interfaces, returning failures for repair rather than
relying on static inspection alone.

### 5.3 Trainability Probe

The trainability probe performs a lightweight single-GPU optimization
run to verify loss reduction and detect numerical issues, nonfinite
gradients, or structural incompatibilities before allocating distributed
training resources. By default, this consists of 30 training steps with
batch size 256. The probe checks whether gradients flow, losses
decrease, and model outputs remain numerically stable.

It also detects saturated or nearly constant outputs and unusually low
initial losses. A decreasing loss trend with positive improvement passes
the loss-reduction check. A 5% relative decrease earns full credit for
this component; smaller positive decreases can still pass.

### 5.4 Full-Scale Distributed Training

After engineer review, candidates advance to full-scale distributed
training on multiple GPUs using production configurations. For
TensorFlow migrations, a warm start from transferred or distilled
parameters can verify task-metric parity through faster convergence.
This offers an early indication that the PyTorch model can recover the
reference model’s quality.

Before downstream deployment, models are trained from a cold start in
the PyTorch pipeline to establish reproducible training lineage
independent of transferred TensorFlow weights. Models with string
features require cold starts because LinkedIn’s TensorFlow and PyTorch
training stacks use different hashing and tokenization transforms,
making direct reuse of feature-dependent weights unreliable
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Stage 2: full-scale training. ‣ 3.1 AutoTorch Model Generation ‣ 3 System Architecture")).

### 5.5 Output Predictions Validation

For high-fidelity model cloning, candidates must accurately reproduce
the source model’s prediction outputs on the same sampled inputs. The
representation evaluated depends on task semantics: logits are compared
for binary classification heads, softmax probabilities for multi-class
heads, and raw prediction scores for ranking models. Evaluating
prediction values rather than discrete class labels catches differences
that label agreement alone would miss.

Output parity ($`P_{\rm io}`$) compares predictions on identical inputs.
For scalar outputs, output parity combines correlation (40%),
tolerance-based agreement (40%; absolute tolerance $`10^{-3}`$, relative
tolerance 1–5%), and near-exact match (20%; absolute difference at most
$`10^{-3}`$). Near-exact matching does not require bitwise equality. For
vector outputs, cosine similarity and near-exact match contribute
equally (50% each).

Stage 1 uses randomly sampled inputs for lightweight distillation and
conversion scoring, without enforcing disjointness between the two
samples. The resulting parity scores guide conversion and iterative
repair rather than serving as independent estimates of model
equivalence. Final task quality is evaluated separately after full-scale
training using the standard offline evaluation pipeline.

### 5.6 Primary-Metric Validation

Task-metric parity ($`P_{\rm task}`$) compares the primary offline
metric of a TensorFlow reference and its PyTorch candidate on the same
data. For AUC, the score is zero if either model performs at or below
chance (0.5). AUC values between 0.5 and 0.55 reduce the parity score to
account for weak predictive signal. Once both AUCs reach 0.55, the
parity score depends only on their closeness: each absolute AUC gap of
0.01 reduces the score by two points from 100, with a floor of zero.

The same principle applies to other task metrics, including NDCG@K,
Precision@K, and Recall@K for ranking, or RMSE for regression. Source
and candidate use the same offline data and metric definition, including
ranking cutoff K. Metric direction and no-signal baselines are
task-specific; the AUC thresholds do not apply to these other metrics.
Stage 1 uses task-metric parity to guide conversion repair. Final task
quality is evaluated separately after full-scale training. For newly
generated models without a source, the task specification provides the
quality target.

### 5.7 Multi-Dimensional Scoring

TensorFlow conversions use the composite score and mandatory checks
defined in
Equation [1](#S3.E1 "In Stage 1: sampled generation and repair. ‣ 3.1 AutoTorch Model Generation ‣ 3 System Architecture").
A conversion qualifies as a high cloning match when its score reaches 90
and the mandatory API and trainability checks pass. Lower-scoring
conversions require explicit engineer approval before Stage 2. The
weights and threshold are fixed in this deployment; we have not
evaluated their sensitivity or calibration against full-training
outcomes.

For new models, there is no reference implementation to compare against.
We instead score trainability (35%), metric achievement (45%), and code
quality (20%) after training. Before full-scale training, the generated
code must pass validity and package/export checks. Post-training
qualification requires the generated model to be trainable, pass API
compliance checks, and meet the task-metric target supplied in its
specification. The target is a minimum for higher-is-better metrics and
a maximum for lower-is-better metrics; no task-independent metric cutoff
is used.

### 5.8 Model Packaging and Handoff

AutoTorch outputs a trainable model bundle containing implementation
code, configurations, evaluation adapters, and export metadata for
downstream productionization or review.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 5: Skills propose architectures, and executable checks return
failure evidence for repair. New-model generation uses separate scoring
after full training.

## 6 Budgeted Model Research

### 6.1 Search Objective and Constraints

AutoResearch searches for model improvements within a fixed wall-clock
time budget. Starting from a validated baseline $`c_{0}`$, it evaluates
candidate changes using the model’s existing training and evaluation
pipeline. The current best model, or incumbent, is updated only after a
round completes. The search returns this incumbent, or the original
model if no round improves it.

### 6.2 Research Direction Search

AutoResearch proposes model changes based on the existing code,
configurations, and previous experiments
(Figure [7](#S6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research")).
Engineers can also specify research directions. Each proposal identifies
the components to change, the expected effect, the target metric, and a
minimal experiment. When improvements plateau, a dedicated skill
explores alternative directions. Search stops when the clock-hour budget
or configured stopping criterion is reached.

### 6.3 Experiment Orchestration

We use an external Python orchestrator to manage the search. It tracks
experiment history, submits parallel training jobs, records metrics, and
maintains the current incumbent.

Each search has a wall-clock time budget and a configurable concurrency
limit, typically four experiments. Results are recorded as trials
finish, but no replacement trial is launched and the incumbent is not
updated until the round completes. The orchestrator then selects the
best candidate that improves the incumbent; otherwise, it keeps the
incumbent. Candidates are selected as complete implementations, without
automatically merging changes from sibling worktrees. Completed-round
results guide the next proposals
(Figure [6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research")).

The time budget includes waiting for slower trials at the round barrier.
This policy trades immediate reuse of idle slots for comparison against
a fixed incumbent. Experiment history persists across agent sessions.

### 6.4 Candidate Evaluation

During search, candidates are ranked against the incumbent using the
pipeline’s primary metric. After search, the selected candidate is
compared with the original baseline on held-out data reserved for final
evaluation \[[3](#bib.bib3)\]. The held-out results do not guide
proposals, incumbent updates, or selection of another candidate. The
improvement results in
Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research")
use this final held-out comparison.

### 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness

Not every failed experiment indicates a bad model. Some failures come
from the training environment, dependencies, or the harness itself.

When this happens, the agent uses the error logs and execution context
to diagnose the issue and propose a fix. Harness changes are submitted
as pull requests and go through normal code review and integration
tests. Successful repairs can also inform future runs through persistent
memory, reducing the need to diagnose the same issue repeatedly.

## 7 Evaluation Methodology

#### Research questions.

We organize deployment observations around three questions: (RQ1) Can
agent loops generate, train, and evaluate models on production ML
infrastructure? (RQ2) How do external control mechanisms enforce
execution and completion constraints? (RQ3) Can agent loops like
AutoResearch improve model quality under fixed clock-hour budgets?

### 7.1 RQ1: ML Framework Migration

Since May 2026, we have used AutoTorch for TensorFlow migration and
XGBoost replacement. Operational completion requires generation and
full-scale training. Quality qualification checks task quality and
applicable cloning criteria only for completed runs.
Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research")
reports completion over all attempts and quality passing over
completions; neither rate measures engineer overrides. Engineers can
reuse code from incomplete runs for debugging and further iteration.

Table [2](#S7.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Migration time. ‣ 7.1 RQ1: ML Framework Migration ‣ 7 Evaluation Methodology")
presents five AutoTorch cases spanning greenfield migration,
TensorFlow-to-PyTorch porting, and tree-to-neural replacement. The
agents delivered PyTorch models and training pipelines, using validation
feedback to repair data processing, evaluation, and architecture
mismatches.

#### Execution latency.

Stage 1 generation and repair took 6.3 hours at p50 and 32 hours at p90.
Among exported models, end-to-end generation to export, including
engineer review, took 2.4 days at p50 and 5.8 days at p90
(Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research")).

#### Migration time.

Engineering teams report that migrating a pipeline with comparable
offline primary-metric quality typically takes eight weeks manually,
compared with two weeks using the agent stack—a $`4\times`$ speedup in
end-to-end migration. The comparison measures elapsed project duration,
not active engineer-hours. Measured AutoTorch export time and estimated
full-project migration duration cover different workflow boundaries.

|  AT-2 |  XGBoost $`\rightarrow`$ TabM; job-posting classification |  Changed loss to per-example binary cross-entropy |  AUC matched |
|  AT-3 |  TensorFlow Ranking-based CTR model |  Ported to PyTorch with weight transfer; fixed data and evaluation mismatches |  AUC matched |
|  AT-4 |  TensorFlow multi-task model (200M embedding parameters) |  Ported to PyTorch; repaired preprocessing, sparse gradients, and task-output handling |  Embedding outputs matched (output-parity check) |
|  AT-5 |  TensorFlow graph neural network |  Ported to a PyTorch GNN; restored node encoder and concatenation combiner |  Downstream classifier AUC matched |
| AutoResearch — model optimization |  |  |  |
|  AR-1 |  GNN connection recommendation |  Reduced encoder to one wider layer; increased neighbor sampling; averaged four inference passes; tuned training |  Recall@1000 $`+9.3\%`$ vs. baseline |
|  AR-2 |  MLP classifier |  Widened hidden layers $`[24,12]\rightarrow[64,32]`$ |  Held-out primary AUC $`+1.20\%`$ vs. baseline |
|  AR-3 |  SLM (0.6B) + MLP classification |  Compared linear, MMoE, PLE, and DCNv2 heads with engineer guidance |  $`p_{\rm click}`$ AUC $`+1.2\%`$ vs. MLP baseline (validation) |

*Notes.* Matching does not imply bitwise equivalence. AT-4 reports
embedding-output parity, not a primary task metric. AR-1 combines
several changes on a fixed evaluation fixture; independent held-out
status is not reported. AR-3 is a task-specific validation result, not
an additional held-out win in
Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research").

Table 2: Selected agent-loop cases (AT: AutoTorch; AR: AutoResearch).
These examples are not randomly sampled.

### 7.2 RQ2: Harness Design for External Control under Constraints

#### Iteration overhead.

Setup and the first scored iteration took 2.5 hours at p50 and 15 hours
at p90, compared with 46 minutes and 3.2 hours for subsequent repair
iterations. The first interval includes model construction and initial
validation, whereas later iterations reuse the initialized workflow.

AutoTorch uses executable hooks to enforce business and platform rules,
including API compliance, trainability, and conversion fidelity. Failed
checks return diagnostic feedback for the next repair iteration.
AutoResearch instead maintains experiment history, candidate selection,
and time budgets in an external Python orchestrator. This keeps
execution state separate from agent reasoning across long-running
experiments and multiple agent sessions
(Figure [8](#S7.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 7.3 RQ3: Agent-Guided Model Optimization ‣ 7 Evaluation Methodology")).

### 7.3 RQ3: Agent-Guided Model Optimization

AutoResearch improved the primary metric on final held-out evaluation in
28 of 100 targeted pipelines
(Table [1](#S6.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 6.5 Self-Repairing Harness ‣ 6 Budgeted Model Research")).
If no candidate improved the search-validation metric, the incumbent was
retained; held-out results were reported separately.

AutoResearch supports two modes of experimentation: expert-steered and
autonomous. Domain experts can guide architectures, training
configurations, and constraints to explore; without that guidance, the
agent uses the model repository, configurations, and previous results to
propose experiments. Both modes use the same iterative search loop.

Table [2](#S7.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Migration time. ‣ 7.1 RQ1: ML Framework Migration ‣ 7 Evaluation Methodology")
shows three AutoResearch cases. For a GNN recommender, AutoResearch
explored 49 trials and identified a configuration that improved
Recall@1000 by 9.3%. Widening an MLP classifier improved held-out AUC by
1.2%. For an SLM (0.6B) engagement model, an engineer used AutoResearch
to compare prediction-head architectures, including
MMoE \[[14](#bib.bib14)\], PLE \[[18](#bib.bib18)\], and
DCNv2 \[[19](#bib.bib19)\], and reported obtaining decisive task-level
results in days rather than weeks of manual exploration. DCNv2 improved
two engagement metrics while meeting the relevance guardrail. These
examples show how domain-expert guidance and agent-generated proposals
can accelerate model experimentation.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 8: Harness-specific execution control. AutoTorch uses hooks to
gate each generate–evaluate–repair iteration. AutoResearch maintains
persistent state and round-end selection externally to agent sessions.

## 8 Related Work

#### Model migration.

Nikolov et al. \[[16](#bib.bib16)\] use playbooks and specialized agents
for TensorFlow-to-JAX migration, evaluating complex internal migrations
with checklist-based LLM judges. Liang et al. \[[12](#bib.bib12)\]
combine in-context examples with source-execution oracles and iterative
debugging for PyTorch-to-JAX migration. Our workflow combines
TensorFlow-to-PyTorch parameter transfer and execution-based
qualification with full-scale training and offline evaluation.

#### ML experimentation agents.

AIDE explores code search for model implementation \[[9](#bib.bib9)\],
MLE-STAR refines pipelines using retrieved
knowledge \[[15](#bib.bib15)\], and Auto-RecSys combines asynchronous
recommendation experiments with persistent memory and a separation
between reasoning guidance and deterministic
execution \[[11](#bib.bib11)\]. Our system combines model generation and
optimization with production training and offline evaluation in a shared
platform.

#### Autonomous research.

Karpathy’s autoresearch uses markdown instructions to guide single-GPU
training experiments \[[10](#bib.bib10)\]. AutoResearch was developed
independently and does not use code from autoresearch. R&D-Agent
separates research planning from implementation and
evaluation \[[20](#bib.bib20)\], while The AI Scientist automates idea
generation and experimental execution \[[13](#bib.bib13)\]. AutoResearch
applies related propose–implement–evaluate loops to existing production
training pipelines, with synchronous parallel trials and a shared
elapsed-time budget.

#### Agent runtimes.

AgentScope provides multi-agent communication and fault
tolerance \[[5](#bib.bib5)\]. The agentic job control plane complements
this by providing isolated sandboxes and brokered access to compute,
production data, and ML platform APIs for long-running workflows.

#### Program search and optimization.

AlphaEvolve couples code changes to automated
evaluation \[[17](#bib.bib17)\]. Random search \[[2](#bib.bib2)\],
Optuna \[[1](#bib.bib1)\], and Vizier \[[6](#bib.bib6)\] provide
fixed-space optimization baselines. Our evaluation uses live production
workloads rather than public benchmarks \[[8](#bib.bib8),
[4](#bib.bib4)\].

## 9 Discussion and Limitations

The agent loops automate substantial parts of model generation and
optimization, but engineers remain responsible for reviewing generated
code, handling model-specific requirements, and making deployment
decisions. Executable validation helps identify numerical and
platform-integration failures, but it cannot establish model equivalence
across all inputs.

A central limitation is potential skew between offline and online task
metrics. Models that match or improve offline metrics can behave
differently under production traffic, shifting data distributions, and
user feedback. Our evaluation covers training and offline model quality;
online serving integration and A/B testing remain outside the scope of
the agent stack.

The system also depends on LinkedIn’s existing preprocessing, training,
and evaluation interfaces. Adapting these agent loops to another ML
platform would require integrating with its corresponding interfaces.

## 10 Conclusion

We presented AutoTorch and AutoResearch, two agent loops for model
generation, framework migration, and optimization within LinkedIn’s
PyTorch training platform. AutoTorch uses executable validation to guide
model generation and repair, while AutoResearch keeps experiment state
across long-running optimization tasks. Engineering teams report a
$`4\times`$ reduction in elapsed migration time while recovering
comparable offline model quality. The stack automates much of this work
while retaining engineer review and established production training
controls.
````
